did_you_know.text: The title attributes the psalm to Asaph and indicates that it is intended for the director of music and associated with Jeduthun. In this way, it presents the psalm as having a musical and liturgical setting.
The psalmist opens with an emphatic repetition of the words “My voice is to God,” stressing that he cries out to God and asks him to listen.
This verse describes ongoing distress: the psalmist turns to the Lord on the day of his trouble, his hand remains outstretched through the night, and his soul refuses to be comforted.
At first, remembering God does not bring calm but causes inner turmoil; the psalmist describes his spirit as overwhelmed and heavy.
The psalmist describes a state of shock and an inability to speak through the words, “I am troubled, and I cannot speak.”
In the midst of his crisis, the psalmist turns to the past: he considers ancient days and bygone years, beginning a movement from personal distress toward the memory of history.
The memory is also connected with music: the psalmist remembers his song in the night and meditates with his heart while searching within his spirit.

In verses 8–10, a series of rhetorical questions asks whether the Lord has rejected his people, whether his steadfast love has ceased, whether his promise has failed, and whether his compassion has been forgotten.
The turning point of the psalm is the decision to remember God’s deeds, his wonders, and his works; memory becomes a source of strength.

The psalm ends with an image of guidance: God leads his people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Thus, the account of deliverance and guidance concludes not with a personal appearance by Moses and Aaron, but with their serving as the hands that lead the people.
